claims.text: First-principles-informed, accurately trained interatomic potentials can predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed predictions can achieve accuracy comparable to calorimetry.
The proposed method operates at a fraction of the computational cost of relevant benchmark approaches.
High-entropy-alloy solid solutions near their melting points exhibit complex multicomponent phase equilibria.
Interatomic potentials or reduced-order models trained on first-principles data can be used to simulate fusion transitions and liquid-phase behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Fusion and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties can be extracted using equilibrium molecular dynamics or related statistical methods.
The quality and transferability of the interatomic potentials determine how well atomic interactions and phase equilibria are represented in multicomponent alloys.
Calibration against first-principles data enables the potentials to capture the energetics of structural rearrangement during melting.
Capturing melting-related structural energetics permits rapid and accurate estimation of fusion thermodynamic properties.

Predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties are expected to agree with experiments or high-fidelity simulations within approximately 5–10%.
The approximately 5–10% performance is expected across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
Traditional DSC and high-temperature phase-diagram methods are more time-consuming than the proposed computational approach.
Traditional approaches, including CALPHAD modeling, can be less accurate in the complex compositional space of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach is expected to be applicable to high-entropy-alloy compositions lying within the training domain of the potentials.
The approach may be unreliable for compositions outside or poorly represented in the training set.
The approach may be unreliable for kinetic regimes that diverge significantly from equilibrium.
Broad experimental validation is required to establish the precise error margins and compositional robustness.
Deviation greater than approximately 10% from experimental measurements across a statistically significant number of in-domain alloy compositions would falsify the approach.
